title: New Orange-Lipped Monkey Found in Congo!
summary:
Imagine a monkey with bright orange lips and spiky hair, like it just put on lipstick for a party. That's the Likweli, a brand-new monkey species discovered in the forests of the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC). It's only the fifth new African monkey found in the past 75 years!

The Likweli is black with a cream-orange patch around its mouth and nose. It has gray cheeks and a white patch near its tail. Adults weigh about 15 pounds — the size of a small dog. They live high in the trees in groups of about six. They usually watch people silently, but their loud, roar-like calls are hard to miss.

An explorer first snapped a blurry photo in 2008. Then the monkey vanished from sight until 2018, when researcher Jean-Pierre Kapale spotted it in Lomami National Park. Over the next years, scientists recorded 114 sightings. But they needed physical evidence to confirm it was a new species. In April 2021, park guards seized three Likweli carcasses — the monkeys had been killed for meat. This let scientists study the monkey closely and collect DNA.

The DNA, features, and calls all proved it was new. They named it Colobus congoensis, meaning 'from Congo.' Its closest relative lives over 700 miles away. Scientists think the two species split from a common ancestor about 4 to 5 million years ago. The findings were published in PLOS One on July 15, 2026.

Now scientists worry about the Likweli's future. It lives in only about 656 square miles, mostly inside the park. It faces threats from hunting and habitat loss. The team proposed it be listed as Endangered to help protect it.
why_it_matters: Finding a brand-new animal today shows how much of nature we still don't know, and it reminds us that protecting forests helps creatures we haven't even met yet.

background_read: The Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) is a big country in Central Africa covered in huge rainforests, and scientists there are still finding animals that no one has ever named.
Scientists use DNA — the tiny coded instructions inside every living thing — to check whether an animal is truly a new species and not just a cousin of one we already know.

When experts say a species is 'Endangered', it means the animal could die out completely, and then governments can make rules to protect it; a worldwide group of scientists called the IUCN keeps the official list of endangered animals.
Article_Structure: WHO: Scientists studying monkeys in the DRC, the researcher Jean-Pierre Kapale who spotted the Likweli, and park guards who seized the carcasses.
WHAT: A brand-new monkey species with orange lips, the Likweli (Colobus congoensis), was confirmed as new to science and given a name.
WHERE: High in the trees of Lomami National Park in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, in an area of only about 656 square miles.
WHY: Its DNA, body features and loud calls proved it was a new species, and the team wants it listed as Endangered so it can be protected from hunting and habitat loss.

perspectives.description: They are thrilled because naming a new monkey is very rare — only the fifth new African monkey found in 75 years — and it took DNA, photos and calls to prove it.
They point out that the Likweli lives in a small area, is hunted for its meat, and is losing forest, so they want it officially listed as Endangered.
For local families the forest is also a place to find food, so new protection rules could change their daily lives, even though most people would not want the monkey to disappear.
